title: Portrait of the Khalsa

segments.voice: Yesterday, the portrait of a gurmukh: humble, truthful, content, serving, remembering. Your line was grow into it. Which trait did you practice where nobody noticed? Day one thousand four hundred ten.

A steel bowl of water and sugar. A double-edged sword stirring it while banis are recited. Five Sikhs, themselves already initiated, conduct the rite, and those coming forward drink the amrit and have it sprinkled on their eyes and hair. From that moment they belong to the Khalsa. Yesterday's portrait was the inner one, a face turned toward the Guru. Today the portrait gets a name, a code and a visible form.
screen: `A STEEL BOWL, A DOUBLE-EDGED SWORD.` → `THE AMRIT.` → `A NAME, A CODE, A FORM.`

segments.voice: First, pure. Sikhs say khalsa means pure. In a savaiya attributed to Guru Gobind Singh, in paraphrase: the one who remembers the ever-living light day and night, who brings no other but the One into the mind, in whose heart the full light shines, know that one as khaalas, pure. Purity here isn't a spotless record. It's a heart with one light in it. Second, brave. The Khalsa is remembered as saint-soldiers: ready to defend the weak, never to bully. Courage in this portrait is aimed outward, at someone else's safety. Third, disciplined. The Khalsa keep the five Ks, keep the daily prayers, and keep a code of conduct, the rehat, that rules out things like tobacco and adultery. It's a discipline you can see on a crowded street: the turban, the kara, the bearing. Fourth, generous. The hands that carry a kirpan also stir the pots in the langar and give a share of what they earn. And an honest note: not every Sikh has taken amrit. Sikhs who haven't are still Sikhs, and for some the Khalsa is a commitment grown toward slowly, when they're ready. Pure, brave, disciplined, generous. Khalsa means pure.
screen: `PURE: ONE LIGHT IN THE HEART.` · `BRAVE: FOR SOMEONE ELSE'S SAFETY.` · `DISCIPLINED: THE REHAT.` · `GENEROUS: THE LANGAR POT.` · then, large: `KHALSA MEANS PURE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: practice one trait. Settle, and breathe. Let the traits pass, one per breath: pure, brave, disciplined, generous. Pick the one that asks the most of you today. Pure might mean one honest motive. Brave, one hard sentence said kindly. Disciplined, one habit kept when it's inconvenient. Generous, one thing given before anyone asks. Breathe with your choice, and picture where it will happen. If you pray, you can offer that moment to God. The bell holds the time.
Portrait of the Khalsa. The initiated community of Sikhs: pure, brave, disciplined, generous, with one light in the heart. Today's word.
Your line: khalsa means pure. Today, do one thing with a single, clean motive, nothing hidden behind it, and notice how light it feels. Day one thousand four hundred ten.

howItsDone: Sikhs who join the Khalsa take amrit in the amrit sanchar ceremony conducted by five initiated Sikhs, then keep the five Ks and the Sikh code of conduct (rehat); Sikhs who have not taken amrit are still Sikhs.

original.note: Gurmukhi: the Khalsa, the initiated community; Sikhs say the word means pure.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Khalsa is a military order from history.
what it means: the Khalsa is the initiated community of Sikhs: pure, brave, disciplined, generous.
what a scholar hears: in the savaiya, the one in whose heart the full light shines is the one to know as khaalas.
